result.summary: Pausanias describes roads out of Argos: to Mantinea with the temple of Aphrodite and Ares, Oenoe and Mount Artemisium; to Lyrceia and Orneae; and toward Epidaurus, with the monument of Proetus and Acrisius, Tiryns, Midea and Lessa. He mixes local legends with notes on ruins.

scenes.title: Road to Mantinea and Oenoe
scenes.summary: A double-entranced temple holds statues of Aphrodite and Ares. Oenoe is named for Oeneus, who died at Argos with Diomede; above lies Mount Artemisium, source of the Inachus.

scenes.title: Lyrceia and Orneae
scenes.summary: Lyrceia is where Lynceus signalled his escape, a memory kept in an annual torch procession. Orneae is named for Orneus and has temples of Artemis and of all the gods.
scenes.stakes: Lynceus must escape Danaus and signal safety to Hypermnestra.

scenes.title: Road to Epidaurus
scenes.summary: A pyramid-like monument marks the drawn battle of Proetus and Acrisius. Pausanias then describes Tiryns' Cyclopean walls, Midea, and Lessa with the altars on Mount Arachnaeum.
scenes.stakes: Proetus and Acrisius fight for supremacy over Argos.

alias_notes.explanation: Older name of the place, before Lyrcus lived there.
Old name of the mountain in Inachus' day.

analysis.text: Place names are explained by founders and heroes, tying the landscape to myth and local pride.
Pausanias records ruins left by Argive conquests of neighbouring cities, such as Tiryns and Orneae.

fun_facts.text: Greeks believed the huge stone walls of Tiryns were built by Cyclopes; they are Bronze Age and still stand.

language_notes.text: Polynices led the Argive expedition of the Seven against Thebes to regain his throne from his brother Eteocles.
"Torrent" means a seasonal stream that flows only in winter; "Ravine" is the name given to it.
Oeneus was Diomede's grandfather through Diomede's father Tydeus, Oeneus's son, hence the grandfatherly care.
The fifty brothers are the sons of Aegyptus, who were killed by the Danaids on their wedding night; Lynceus was spared by Hypermnestra.
A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 180-190 metres, so 60 stades is about 11 km.
Homer's catalogue is the list of ships and contingents in the Iliad, Book 2.
"Naturalized" means admitted as citizens of Argos.
"Argolic" means belonging to the Argolid, the region around Argos. The shields are a design carved on the monument.
"Aggrandize Argos" means to enlarge and strengthen Argos by adding the Tirynthians to its population.
The Cyclopes were mythical giants. Greeks attributed massive prehistoric walls to them, since later people could not imagine moving such stones.
"Dovetail" means the small stones were fitted into the gaps between the large blocks to make the wall tight.
The daughters of Prœtus were, in myth, driven mad; the chambers are traditionally linked with them.
Inachus was the legendary first king of Argos and river god, so this marks a very remote age.

context_notes.text: Pausanias often describes temples as he walks a route, moving from one landmark to the next.
The Inachus was the chief river of the Argolid, named for a legendary river-god and early king.
Torch festivals were common in Greek religion, commemorating a founding event through a repeated ritual.
Menestheus led the Athenian contingent to Troy in the Trojan War.
Prœtus and Acrisius were legendary brothers and rival kings of the Argolid, said to have quarrelled even in the womb.
Electryon, king of Mycenaean Midea, was the father of Alcmena, who became mother of Heracles.
Offering sacrifice to Zeus, the sky and weather god, for rain was a common Greek practice in drought.

literary_notes.text: The flat, dismissive remark shows Pausanias as a selective traveller-guide who reports only what he finds worth seeing.
The lovers' signal fires turn a story of murder into one of survival, joined by fire across the landscape.
The shared tomb for fellow citizens and kinsmen gives the civil strife a sorrowful, humane touch amid plain reporting.
The terse statement that only the site remains contrasts with Midea's earlier royal past mentioned just before.
